Senses.Explanation: Literally, "just as for" (只如). Across Chan discourse and case commentary it is a grammatical pivot: a speaker provisionally leaves the preceding statement in place, selects a concrete case or condition, and reopens questioning. Yuanwu moves from a claim about a world that is entirely a diamond eye to "just as for... how do you observe it?" (只如……且作麼生觀), and elsewhere from passing beyond form and sound to "just as for... how is a message conveyed?" (只如……如何通信). Lamp commentary uses it to press whether Vajra-Equality saw the obstructing demon king, to turn from a general claim to Mazu's exact words, and even to compare the issue with having eaten and walking down the east or west corridor. The imperial birthday addresses likewise move from ceremonial description to "just as for the people of the Way in the forest... how is the line raised?" (只如林下道人……一句如何舉唱). There is no special lexical departure from the ordinary connective; its Chan value is the repeatedly attested dialogue structure of concession or setup followed by a pointed case-question.
Senses.Note: The phrase has 4,021 hits in 321 allowlisted texts. It is overwhelmingly connective rather than a technical headword. Common continuations include 'how?' (如何), 'what about it?' (作麼生), 'what do you say?' (且道), and a named earlier saying or case. The curated occurrences come from discourse, lamp commentary, and a formal high-seat address.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如盡華藏世界海。窮虛空邊際。都盧是箇金剛眼。且作麼生觀。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu uses the pivot to turn a claim about the whole world as a diamond eye into the question of how to observe it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如透出形聲。且道。如何通信。還委悉麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate Yuanwu discourse pivots from passing beyond form and sound to asking how a message is conveyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如金剛齊，還見障蔽魔王麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Joint Lamp commentary turns to the named Vajra-Equality case and asks whether he saw the obstructing demon king.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如儞喫了飯，東廊上，西廊下，不可總問人得與不得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Joint Lamp encounter uses the pivot for the concrete comparison of eating and then walking down either corridor.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如林下道人共樂昇平，同歸化育一句如何舉唱？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An imperial birthday address pivots from ceremonial praise to asking how the line for forest-dwelling people of the Way is raised.

Senses.Explanation: A verb-object phrase: "raise" or "hold upright" (竪) the whisk (拂), usually the master's fly-whisk (拂子). This seeded graph form occurs 471 times in 90 allowlisted texts; the common orthographic form with the other graph for "raise" (豎拂) occurs 2,438 times. The corpus records the action as a direct answer, as a demonstration followed by lowering the whisk, and as a recurrent action whose import students ask about. Nanta Guangyong answers "who is Manjusri's teacher?" by raising the whisk to show him (如何是文殊師；師竪拂子示之). Zhaozhou raises the whisk when asked whether he will receive "the person who sets the realm in order" (撥亂乾坤底人來，師還接否；師竪拂子). Yunmen raises the older Zifu exchange in which a monk asks, "what is the import of the ancients picking up the mallet and raising the whisk?" (古人拈槌竪拂意旨如何). A later Deshan record explicitly classifies "raise a finger and raise the whisk" as a dead phrase (舉指竪拂，是死句). These records do not give the raised whisk one uniform gloss, and this entry does not add one.
Senses.Note: The two orthographic forms, the older graph for "raise" (竪) and its dominant variant (豎), do not create a second sense. Corpus counts: "raise the whisk" with the seeded spelling (竪拂), 471; "raise the whisk" with the dominant spelling (豎拂), 2,438; "raise the fly-whisk" (竪拂子), 189; "raise up the fly-whisk" (竪起拂子), 492; "pick up the mallet and raise the whisk" (拈槌竪拂), 108; "raise a finger and raise the whisk" (舉指竪拂), 4. The seeded SourceTerm is retained for ID stability, while the dominant written variant is documented here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰如何是文殊師。師竪拂子示之。僧曰。莫遮箇是麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Nanta Guangyong section of the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp: a monk asks, "who is Manjusri's teacher?" The master raises the whisk to show him; the monk asks, "is it not this?" Nanta Guangyong has no roster link used here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃竪起拂子云。只這是要知示現受生麼。竪拂子云。只這是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Yuanwu Keqin's fourth informal address: he raises the whisk and says, "just this is it"; asks whether they want to know manifestation and receiving birth; then raises the whisk and again says, "just this is it."

Occurrences.Kwic: 師竪拂子。僧曰。恁麼則得遇明君去也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Zhaozhou Congshen's section of the Compendium of Five Lamps. After a monk asks whether he will receive one who sets the realm in order, Zhaozhou raises the whisk; the monk replies, "then I have met a wise ruler."

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉僧問資福。古人拈槌竪拂意旨如何。福云。古人與麼那。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen's chamber sayings raise a Zifu case: a monk asks Zifu, "what is the import of the ancients picking up the mallet and raising the whisk?" Zifu replies, "did the ancients do that?" MasterName is null because this is an explicitly raised two-speaker case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 揚眉瞬目，舉指竪拂，是死句。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Deshan Yuanmi section of the Strict Lineage of Five Lamps: "raise the brows and blink the eyes; raise a finger and raise the whisk—these are dead phrases." The exact section master lacks a validated roster link used here.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "existing in oneself" or "being at one's own disposal" (自在): "free and at ease," "unconstrained," or adverbially "freely," attested 4,537 times in 388 allowlisted texts. A record closes an address with "everyone drink tea in the hall, free and at ease" (堂中喫茶，自由自在). Another says, "only upon arriving here can one roll up and extend freely, with response and function unimpaired" (卷舒自在，應用無虧). A later compilation uses the result phrase "obtain great freedom" (獲大自在), while Zhe'an Fan says "unconstrained and unbound in every place; without fault at every time" (一切處自在無繫，一切時無所過患). Dahui says, "then one enters birth and death and obtains great freedom" (出生入死得大自在). Other records say one can be freely at ease at every time and place, pair freedom in birth and death with freedom in coming and going, and explicitly test whether freedom at death matches ordinary freedom amid encountered objects. The word thus appears as adjective, adverb, result noun, and reduplicated "free and at ease" (自由自在), without requiring a further religious abstraction.
Senses.Note: Counted constructions: "free and at ease" (自由自在), 185; "free and unobstructed" (自在無礙), 50; "obtain great freedom" (得大自在), 258; "not at ease" (不自在), 134. The compound personal/title name "Contemplating Freely" (觀自在, 278) and personal names such as Yun Zizai are proper-name uses and are not merged into this adjectival sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 各自大家堂中喫茶自由自在
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Address ending: "everyone drink tea in the hall, free and at ease." The governing speaker is not roster-linked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 到這裏始能卷舒自在，應用無虧
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen Lingkan's section: "only upon arriving here can one roll up and extend freely, with response and function unimpaired." No validated roster link is used.

Occurrences.Kwic: 境智融通，色空無礙，獲大自在
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compilation prose: "objects and knowing interpenetrate; form and space are unobstructed; obtain great freedom."

Occurrences.Kwic: 一切處自在無繫，一切時無所過患。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhe'an Fan: "unconstrained and unbound in every place; without fault at every time."

Occurrences.Kwic: 則出生入死得大自在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's address: "then one enters birth and death and obtains great freedom."

Occurrences.Kwic: 便乃一切時一切處。任運自在。應用無方。諸人還委悉麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's record says: 'at every time and in every place, proceed freely and at ease, responding without fixed direction,' then asks whether the assembly understands.

Occurrences.Kwic: 透得一句生死自在；透得二句來去自由；三句透得，可以為人天師；四句總透得，可以為佛祖師。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An enumerated address pairs being free in birth and death after penetrating one phrase with free coming and going after two.

Occurrences.Kwic: 當知欲驗臨終受生自在不自在，但驗尋常行心於塵境自由不自由。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A compilation gives an explicit test: whether one is free at death is checked against whether one's ordinary conduct is free amid encountered objects.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛秖是去住自由，不同眾生。佛不是虗空受苦，何得不苦？若說不苦，此語違負。等閑莫說，錯說佛神通自在不自在。具慙愧人，不敢說佛是有為是無為，不敢說佛自由不自由。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record cautions against casually declaring whether a buddha is free or not free, pairing that restraint with refusing to call a buddha conditioned or unconditioned.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, one's own nature, or the nature belonging to the subject under discussion. The expression occurs 2,091 times in 260 allowlisted texts. The Platform Record says that one's own nature is originally clean, contains the ten thousand things, and is not apart from them; another recension lists it as originally clean, not arising or perishing, complete in itself, unmoving, and able to produce the ten thousand things. These are the record's predicates, not an imported definition. Other Chan records use the term in questions about seeing, clarifying, or being unaware of one's own nature. One discourse says that what is reluctantly named the naturally true buddha of one's own nature is also called the master of one's own house. Direct answers do not settle into a single formula: asked 'What is one's own nature?' one master says, 'I will not say'; asked about the naturally true buddha of one's own nature while tending a fire, another tells the monk to bring a bundle of firewood.
Senses.Note: The possessive force varies with the grammatical subject: a person's own nature, or the nature of a thing. The mirror record supplies 605 of the 2,091 hits, so the entry balances its evidence with the Platform Record, lamp material, and individual discourse records. The named compound 'accomplished own-nature' receives a later text's separate body-and-function classification and is not used to redefine every bare occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 起六識：眼識、耳識、鼻識、舌識、身識、意識，六門、六塵。自性含萬法，名為含藏識。思量即轉識，生六識，出六門、六塵，是三六十
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An early Platform Record recension says that one's own nature contains the ten thousand things and names the resulting inclusive designation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後向甚麼處去？師曰，千株松下，百草頭邊。師燒火次，僧問，如何是自性天真佛。師曰，與我搬一束柴來。僧肩柴至，又問。師曰，者奴子好惡

Occurrences.Kwic: 而生其心語，祖於言下大徹，遂啟五祖曰：一切萬法不離自性，何期自性本自清淨？何期自性本不生滅？何期自性本自具足？何期自性本無動搖？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later record quotes Huineng's list of four predicates for one's own nature and begins by saying that all things are not apart from it.
